result.markdown: --- title: "Model development and specification" format: html: number-sections: true toc: true toc-depth: 3 crossref: tbl-title: "Table S" tbl-prefix: "Table S" editor: visual --- # Model development and selection ## Candidate models We considered eight candidate models, starting with a baseline model and progressively adding interaction terms. The candidate models differed in their inclusion of interactions between sex, air temperature, and relative humidity. An overview of the candidate models and their respective interaction terms is provided in Table 1. **Table 1. Overview of the candidate models.** | Model | Interaction terms | |:------|:------------------| | `mod_00` | None (baseline) | | `mod_01` | Air temperature × relative humidity | | `mod_02` | Sex × air temperature | | `mod_03` | Sex × relative humidity | | `mod_04` | Sex × air temperature; air temperature × relative humidity | | `mod_05` | Sex × relative humidity; air temperature × relative humidity | | `mod_06` | Sex × air temperature; sex × relative humidity | | `mod_07` | Sex × air temperature; sex × relative humidity; air temperature × relative humidity | ## Model comparison We initially compared the predictive performance of the candidate models using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO), based on the expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD). Higher ELPD values indicate better expected predictive performance. The reliability of the LOO estimates was assessed using Pareto-$k$ diagnostics. Because some models exhibited Pareto-$k$ values exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.7, we additionally performed stratified 10-fold cross-validation to obtain a more robust assessment of predictive performance. The folds were stratified by condition, and model performance was evaluated on held-out observations. The results of the LOO comparison and the stratified 10-fold cross-validation are presented in @tbl-loo-comparison and @tbl-kfold-comparison, respectively. We also assessed the consistency between the two approaches by comparing their model rankings using Spearman's rank correlation. **Table 2. Comparison of candidate models based on approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO).** | Model | ELPD difference | SE difference | ELPD LOO | Pareto-$k$ diagnostic | |:------|----------------:|--------------:|---------:|:----------------------| | `mod_01` | 0.000 | 0.000 | -2320.52 | 8 observations > 0.7 | | `mod_05` | -0.562 | 2.381 | -2321.08 | 5 observations > 0.7 | | `mod_07` | -0.568 | 2.619 | -2321.09 | 7 observations > 0.7 | | `mod_04` | -0.917 | 1.179 | -2321.43 | 7 observations > 0.7 | | `mod_00` | -1.987 | 3.829 | -2322.50 | 7 observations > 0.7 | | `mod_03` | -2.242 | 4.019 | -2322.76 | 4 observations > 0.7 | | `mod_06` | -3.596 | 4.114 | -2324.11 | 4 observations > 0.7 | | `mod_02` | -4.178 | 3.861 | -2324.70 | 7 observations > 0.7 | ::: {#tbl-supp-risk-prediction-heating2 .cell tbl-cap='Posterior predictive probabilities (posterior mean and 95% credible intervals) of TSV categories for heating intervention. comparisons, we selected `mod_01` as the final model. This model included an interaction between air temperature and relative humidity, in addition to the main effects and the condition-varying effects. Its full specification and prior distributions are described in the following sections. # Model specification ## Multinomial logit model Thermal sensation votes (TSV) were recorded on a seven-point ordinal scale ranging from $-3$ (cold) to $+3$ (hot), with $0$ representing the comfortable category. The data consist of 720 observations across 72 experimental conditions. Each observation represents the TSV counts of five participants of the same biological sex under a given combination of experimental conditions. Because individual participant identifiers were unavailable, the model was fitted to aggregated category counts rather than individual-level repeated measurements. The response for observation $i$ is represented by a seven-dimensional count vector: $$ \mathbf Y_i = (Y_{i,-3},Y_{i,-2},Y_{i,-1},Y_{i,0},Y_{i,+1},Y_{i,+2},Y_{i,+3}) \tag{1} $$ where the counts sum to five: $$ \sum_{k=-3}^{+3}Y_{i,k}=5 \tag{2} $$ The response vector is modelled using a multinomial likelihood: $$ \mathbf Y_i \sim \operatorname{Multinomial} \left(5,\mathbf p_i\right) \tag{3} $$ where $\mathbf p_i$ is the vector of probabilities for the seven TSV categories. The comfortable category ($\mathrm{TSV}=0$) is used as the reference category. Its linear predictor is fixed to zero: $$ \eta_{i,0}=0 \tag{4} $$ For the six non-reference categories, the category probabilities are obtained through the softmax transformation: $$ p_{i,k} = \frac{\exp(\eta_{i,k})} {1+\displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal K}\exp(\eta_{i,\ell})}, \qquad k\in\mathcal K \tag{5} $$ where $\mathcal K=\{-3,-2,-1,+1,+2,+3\}$. The probability of the comfortable category is consequently $$ p_{i,0} = \frac{1} {1+\displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal K} \exp(\eta_{i,\ell})} \tag{6} $$ The linear predictor for each non-reference category $k$ is specified as $$ \begin{aligned} \eta_{i,k} =& \alpha_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{sex}[i],k} + \beta_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{t.onset},k} \operatorname{mo}_k(\mathrm{t.onset}_i) + \beta_{\mathrm{t.day},k}\mathrm{t.day}_i \\ &+ \beta_{\mathrm{temp},k}\mathrm{temp}_i + \beta_{\mathrm{hum},k}\mathrm{hum}_i + \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum},k}(\mathrm{temp}_i\mathrm{hum}_i) \end{aligned} \tag{7} $$ Here, $k$ indexes the non-reference TSV categories, $\mathrm{sex}[i]$ identifies the biological sex of observation $i$, and $\mathrm{condition}[i]$ identifies its experimental condition. The variable $\mathrm{t.day}_{i}$ represents the time-of-day indicator (afternoon/evening), while $\mathrm{t.onset}_i$ denotes the ordered level of time since onset for observation $i$, and $\operatorname{mo}_k(\mathrm{t.onset}_i)$ represents its category-specific monotonic effect. The variable $\mathrm{temp}_{i}$ is centred air temperature, and $\mathrm{hum}_{i}$ is centred relative humidity expressed in 5% units. The temperature–humidity interaction is represented by their product. ## Multilevel structure The sex coefficients and the monotonic time-since-onset coefficients are allowed to vary across experimental conditions. The condition-specific effects are decomposed into a constant (population-level) and condition-specific deviations: $$ \alpha_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{sex}[i],k} = \bar{\alpha}_{\mathrm{sex}[i],k} + v_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{sex}[i],k} \tag{8} $$ $$ \beta_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{t.onset},k} = \bar{\beta}_{\mathrm{t.onset},k} + v_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{t.onset},k} \tag{9} $$ Here, $\bar{\alpha}_{\mathrm{sex}[i],k}$ and $\bar{\beta}_{\mathrm{t.onset},k}$ represent the constant (population-level) coefficients for the corresponding sex and monotonic time-since-onset effect, respectively. The terms $v_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{sex}[i],k}$ and $v_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{t.onset},k}$ represent condition-specific deviations from these constant (population-level) coefficients. This hierarchical structure allows partial pooling across experimental conditions. The condition-varying effects are jointly modelled. For each condition $j$ (with $j=1,\ldots,72$ indexing the 72 experimental conditions), the vector of deviations is defined as $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf v_j = (& v_{j,\mathrm{male},-3}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},-3}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},-3}, \\ & v_{j,\mathrm{male},-2}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},-2}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},-2}, \\ & v_{j,\mathrm{male},-1}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},-1}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},-1}, \\ & v_{j,\mathrm{male},+1}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},+1}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},+1}, \\ & v_{j,\mathrm{male},+2}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},+2}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},+2}, \\ & v_{j,\mathrm{male},+3}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},+3}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},+3} )^\mathsf T \end{aligned} \tag{10} $$ Thus, each condition has a vector of 18 condition-varying effects, jointly modelled according to $$ \mathbf v_j \sim \operatorname{MVN} \left( \mathbf 0_{18},\boldsymbol\Sigma_{18\times18} \right), \qquad j=1,\ldots,72 \tag{11} $$ where $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{18\times18}$ is an $18\times18$ covariance matrix. This structure allows correlations between condition-varying effects across sexes, monotonic onset coefficients, and TSV categories. ### Non-centred parameterisation For computational efficiency, the multivariate normal distribution of the condition-varying effects is implemented using a non-centred parameterisation. First, the standardised condition effects are defined as $$ \mathbf z_j \sim \operatorname{MVN} \left( \mathbf 0,\mathbf I_{18} \right), \qquad j=1,\ldots,72 \tag{12} $$ where $\mathbf I_{18}$ is the $18\times18$ identity matrix. The condition-varying effects are then obtained through the transformation $$ \mathbf v_j = \mathbf D_{\sigma} \mathbf L_{\Omega} \mathbf z_j, \qquad j=1,\ldots,72 \tag{13} $$ where $\mathbf D_{\sigma}$ is a diagonal matrix containing the group-level standard deviations, and $\mathbf L_{\Omega}$ is the Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix $\boldsymbol\Omega$. The covariance matrix is therefore expressed as $$ \boldsymbol\Sigma = \mathbf D_{\sigma} \boldsymbol\Omega \mathbf D_{\sigma}, \qquad \boldsymbol\Omega = \mathbf L_{\Omega} \mathbf L_{\Omega}^{\mathsf T} \tag{14} $$ This parameterisation ensures that the condition-varying effects follow the multivariate normal distribution specified in Equation (11). ## Monotonic effect of time since onset The effect of time since onset is modelled as a monotonic effect rather than assuming equal spacing between its ordered levels. Let $D$ denote the number of ordered levels of time since onset, and let $\mathrm{t.onset}_i\in\{1,\ldots,D\}$ denote the corresponding level for observation $i$. For each non-reference TSV category $k$, the monotonic effect is defined as $$ \operatorname{mo}_k(\mathrm{t.onset}_i) = (D-1) \sum_{d=1}^{D-1} \zeta_{k,d}\mathbb I(\mathrm{t.onset}_i>d) \tag{15} $$ where $\mathbb I(\cdot)$ is the indicator function and $\boldsymbol\zeta_k$ is a category-specific simplex vector. The simplex weights satisfy $$ \zeta_{k,d}\geq0, \qquad \sum_{d=1}^{D-1}\zeta_{k,d}=1 \tag{16} $$ The simplex weights determine how the overall monotonic effect is distributed across successive levels of time since onset. The scaling factor $D-1$ ensures that the monotonic effect ranges from zero at the first level to $D-1$ at the final level. Each non-reference TSV category has its own simplex vector: $$ \boldsymbol\zeta_k \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet} (\boldsymbol\gamma_k), \qquad k\in\mathcal K \tag{17} $$ where $\boldsymbol\gamma_k$ denotes the vector of prior concentration parameters for category $k$. The simplex weights are category-specific but are shared across experimental conditions. Condition-specific variation in the time-since-onset effect is captured by the corresponding condition-varying regression coefficient in Equation (9). ## Prior specification ### Constant (population-level) regression coefficients #### Biological sex The sex-specific baseline coefficients have category-dependent prior means: $$ \begin{aligned} \bar\alpha_{\mathrm{male}, -3},\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{female}, -3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-2.69,2)\\ \bar\alpha_{\mathrm{male}, -2},\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{female}, -2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-1.84,2)\\ \bar\alpha_{\mathrm{male}, -1},\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{female}, -1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-0.89,2) \\ \bar\alpha_{\mathrm{male}, 1},\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{female}, 1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-0.89,2) \\ \bar\alpha_{\mathrm{male}, 2},\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{female}, 2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-1.84,2)\\ \bar\alpha_{\mathrm{male}, 3},\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{female}, 3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-2.69,2) \end{aligned} \tag{18} $$ #### Time since onset The monotonic time since onset coefficients have the prior: $$ \begin{aligned} \bar\beta_{\mathrm{t.onset}, -3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \bar\beta_{\mathrm{t.onset}, -2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \bar\beta_{\mathrm{t.onset}, -1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \bar\beta_{\mathrm{t.onset}, 1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \bar\beta_{\mathrm{t.onset}, 2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \bar\beta_{\mathrm{t.onset}, 3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25) \end{aligned} \tag{19} $$ Each non-reference TSV category has its own simplex parameter: $$ \begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{-3} \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,2,2,2)\\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{-2} \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,2,2,2)\\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{-1} \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,2,2,2)\\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{1} \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,2,2,2)\\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{2} \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,2,2,2)\\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}_{3} \sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,2,2,2)\\ \end{aligned} \tag{20} $$ The Dirichlet prior is symmetric, assigning equal prior concentration to each increment of the monotonic effect. #### Time of day The time-of-day coefficients have the priors: $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{\mathrm{t.day}, -3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{t.day}, -2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{t.day}, -1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{t.day}, 1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{t.day}, 2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{t.day}, 3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25) \end{aligned} \tag{21} $$ #### Air temperature The air temperature coefficients have the priors: $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{\mathrm{temp}, -3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-1,0.5)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp}, -2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-1,0.5)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp}, -1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-1,0.5)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp}, 1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(1,0.5)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp}, 2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(1,0.5)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp}, 3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(1,0.5) \end{aligned} \tag{22} $$ #### Relative humidity The relative humidity coefficients have the priors: $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{\mathrm{hum}, -3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-0.5,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{hum}, -2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-0.5,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{hum}, -1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-0.5,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{hum}, 1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0.5,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{hum}, 2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0.5,0.25)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{hum}, 3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0.5,0.25) \end{aligned} \tag{23} $$ #### Air temperature and relative humidity interaction The air temperature and relative humidity interaction coefficients have the priors: $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum}, -3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.2)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum}, -2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.2)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum}, -1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.2)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum}, 1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.2)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum}, 2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.2)\\ \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum}, 3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.2) \end{aligned} \tag{24} $$ ### Condition-varying effects The standard deviations of the condition-varying effects are assigned exponential priors: $$ \sigma_r \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(1), \qquad r=1,\ldots,18 \tag{25} $$ where the index $r$ identifies the 18 dimensions of the condition-varying effects vector. The correlation matrix is assigned an LKJ prior: $$ \boldsymbol\Omega \sim \operatorname{LKJ}(2) \tag{26} $$ The standardised effects used in the non-centred parameterisation have independent standard normal priors: $$ z_{j,r} \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,1), \qquad j=1,\ldots,72, \qquad r=1,\ldots,18 \tag{27} $$
